2.text: Many rich reindeer-breeders who have two or more herds do keep a separate

3.text: wife with each herd. ᴇttɪˊhɪn, for example, to whom I have referred before,
3.note: fine — looked, the print supports it

4.text: had two herds, and a wife attending to each. Eiˊheli, on the Oloi River,

5.text: who has also been mentioned before, was the owner of four herds, with as

6.text: many wives looking after them. Omrêlqoˊt, also on the Oloi River, had

7.text: three herds and three wives. Many other reindeer-owners, however, have

8.text: only one wife, their surplus herds being kept by sons, brothers-in-law, brothers,

9.text: and other relatives. On the other hand, many of those who have but one

10.text: herd have at the same time two and more wives, all living in the same camp.

11.text: It appeared from the census figures that the number of men having two and

12.text: more wives reached about fifteen per cent of the total number of married men,

13.text: and in some localities even twenty-five per cent. At the same time, the num-

14.text: ber of rich breeders with two and more herds scarcely reaches three per cent.

15.text: Only a very small number of men have more than two wives. Some

16.text: striking exceptions occur, however. Thus Eiˊheli, referred to above, had four

17.text: living wives, besides four who were dead, and who left him children. He

18.text: had, moreover, one vagrant wife, the old Čaˊkɪhêt, who would live in one

19.text: of his camps part of the time, and would then leave for strange camps some-

20.text: times a hundred miles away. Eiˊheli himself, and all his wives, were old, so

21.text: that jealousy was out of the question. Čaˊkɪhêt had no children, and there-

22.text: fore nothing to bind her to one place. At the same time, her fifty years

23.text: did not prevent her from being a strong woman and an excellent worker.

24.text: She was an expert at dressing skins and sewing garments, which made her

25.text: a welcome guest wherever she went. Finally, her nature was such that she

26.text: could not have been easily persuaded to stay at a place unless she herself

27.text: cared to stay. Thus Čaˊkɪhêt, who had performed the marriage-rite with

28.text: Eiˊheli and had for many years been considered his wife, was still perfectly

29.text: free to satisfy her nomadic instincts. The total number of Eiˊheli’s children

30.text: by all his wives was over twenty, excluding those who had died.

31.text: The Chukchee Mêwêˊtirg̣ɪn, on the Dry Anui River, had at one time

32.text: seven wives in three different camps; later, however, he became poor, and

33.text: his wives deserted him. The Chukchee Nomg̣aˊʟê, on the same river, had

34.text: three wives and fourteen children, almost all of them very young. Another

35.text: rather poor Chukchee, Tomg̣anêˊntɪñ, who also lived on the same river, had

36.text: for a time four wives, all living in the same camp in two tents. Other men,

37.text: well-to-do as well as poor, might be cited who had three and four wives at

39.text: When a Chukchee has two wives living in one camp, he tries to give

40.text: them separate tents, or at least separate sleeping-places in one tent; but I

41.text: have also met bigamists who lived in one sleeping-room with both wives, and

42.text: slept with them under a common cover, the husband lying between the two
